extracted.intended_audience: Anyone in the U.S. who wants to organize locally to protect democracy (new or existing Indivisible group members/leaders)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, local organizing guidance for forming, running, and coordinating volunteer Indivisible groups to resist anti-democratic policies and protect elections over the next two years. Includes strategic priorities (three big plays), operational advice for groups, and recommended state/local actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a local leader; don’t wait for orders
rubrics_metrics.description: Join or form a local Indivisible group or review this guide with your existing group, and start putting the parts of this into action that make sense for where you live. Don’t wait for orders and don’t ask for permission. If you’re in, you’re a leader in this movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act with initiative: pick actions appropriate to your geography and leverage, be entrepreneurial in building activities, and treat every member as a leader. Example admonition: 'Don’t wait for orders and don’t ask for permission.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage constituent power
rubrics_metrics.description: Your power comes from your ability to be a source of support (or a pain in the ass) to those electeds. Constituent power is the ability to reward or punish electeds between elections through organized public pressure, support, or withdrawal of support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the mechanisms: elections, accountability, local reputation. Organize to influence electeds’ incentives—make them fear reputational harm or hope for electoral support. Use public pressure strategically to shift behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus energy where constituent power actually works
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus your energy where your local and state political landscape gives you meaningful leverage—this will vary (MAGA rep/blue governor, blue dot in red state, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map local context before acting. Choose targets (local, state, federal) based on where organized constituent pressure can change outcomes. The guide emphasizes adapting tactics to local conditions rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand what your elected cares about (reelection & reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Electeds care first and foremost about getting reelected and growing their own power; they want constituents to think ‘My elected cares about me, shares my values, and is working hard for me.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft actions that affect an elected’s local standing—threaten reputation in the district, present public narratives about their responsiveness, and demonstrate organized local constituency views to influence votes or statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick strategic national battles to say NO to Project 2025
rubrics_metrics.description: Select national fights where you can stop harm, defend democratic institutions, or energize and fracture political coalitions—fight to win, to delay, or to land a political blow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize fights that (a) stop concrete harm, (b) build national backlash, or (c) are winnable/delayable. Expected outcomes include delay/distraction, occasional wins, and building national backlash. Be prepared for fast initial moves by the administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push Democrats to maintain public, lockstep opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Where you’ve got a Democratic representative/senator, push them to be active fighters against harmful federal agenda items—support, cheerlead, or publicly berate as needed to keep them fighting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use loud, public tactics (letters, calls, local events, op-eds) to keep Democratic electeds accountable to opposition. Emphasize the strategic need for unified Democratic resistance to deny the administration bipartisan cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold vulnerable Republicans publicly accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have a vulnerable Republican rep/senator up in 2026, make them publicly explain their positions and demonstrate that their constituents oppose the worst elements of Project 2025.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create local pressure and visibility: demand public appearances, require position statements, amplify dissent in their districts, and make them fear general election consequences as well as primary threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the local story when reps are safely GOP
rubrics_metrics.description: If your representative/senator is in a safe Republican seat, focus on local storytelling and awareness—short-term pressure may have limited effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and publicize local impacts of federal policies, build narratives in your community, and accept that shifting votes in the short term may be unlikely, but community narrative-building still matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use blue-state/city/local powers aggressively (play hardball)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Democrats control state or local offices, push them to use their executive and legislative powers to protect residents and resist federal policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask state leaders to sign protective executive orders, form interstate alliances, use procurement and economic leverage, decline harmful federal program participation, and enact sanctuary or protective policies. The guide lists many concrete options for states/cities to leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign executive orders and use gubernatorial authority to protect residents
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage Democratic governors to issue executive orders that directly counter federal actions—e.g., protections for immigrants, expanding reproductive healthcare access, enforcing stricter environmental standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive orders can create immediate state-level protections and signaling. Push governors to act early and boldly on areas where they have authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form alliances and interstate compacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Urge governors and AGs to join regional compacts on issues like climate, data privacy, and healthcare to unify state-level resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State alliances amplify policy impact, create legal and economic coordination, and make it harder for federal rollbacks to fully unwind state-level protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use state economic leverage against MAGA-friendly corporate behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: States can set procurement and contracting standards to reward progressive values and refuse to do business with companies that enable MAGA policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate that states use purchasing power and economic policy to advance civil rights, labor, and environmental standards—both substantively protective and politically persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decline to implement certain federal policies where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If federal programs depend on state implementation, urge governors/officials to refuse participation in programs that would enable harm (e.g., police crackdowns, corporate loopholes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify federal opt-outs and campaign for non-participation where ethically or politically necessary to protect residents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt sanctuary and protective local policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities and states should adopt sanctuary policies protecting out-of-state visitors (e.g., for reproductive or gender-affirming care) and expand local protections for vulnerable communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push city councils and county governments to pass ordinances that create real, enforceable protections and make locales safe havens for targeted individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create state-funded legal defense funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate for legal funds to help residents targeted by federal policies (e.g., immigrants at risk of deportation, families losing healthcare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These funds provide immediate relief, deter overreach, and signal state commitment—encourage state legislatures and governors to fund such programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue policies that make Democratic areas demonstrably better places to live
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage state and local Democrats to implement policies that improve quality of life—making Democratic governance a visible alternative to MAGA rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy wins at state/local level (affordable housing, labor protections, climate actions) serve both substantive and political goals: protect residents and strengthen Democratic narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect and win elections (prioritize 2026 infrastructure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work to ensure free and fair 2026 elections and win key state/local offices (governors, secretaries of state, state legislatures, House races) because those winners will administer the 2028 election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on defending against election subversion, recruiting and campaigning for key offices, and using state/federal pressure to hold bad actors accountable. Local organizing, tracking election officials, and publicizing problematic actions are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defend against election subversion in swing states
rubrics_metrics.description: In swing states with an ongoing threat of election subversion, organize locally to track officials, publicize actions, and prepare to stop bureaucratic/technical schemes to subvert elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find who runs your local board of elections, research their record and election calendar, connect with Protect Democracy resources, and build local coalitions focused on procedural defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose local election activities with clear strategic aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Before acting in 2025, ask whether an activity strengthens future Democratic candidates, weakens future Republican opponents, or builds a base of active people for 2026.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize actions that (a) recruit and retain activists, (b) prepare the ground for candidacies, or (c) target vulnerabilities in opposition candidates; treat it as 'choose-your-own-adventure' based on local needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize to protect communities under threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand in solidarity with targeted communities and organize mutual aid and protection—broad-based opposition increases the cost of repression and protects individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create networks of support, public visibility, and rapid response to threats. Emphasize that solidarity is both moral and strategic: widespread opposition makes repression costlier and less likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operate under authoritarian creep (manage risk thoughtfully)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare to operate under increasing authoritarian conditions: determine acceptable personal and group risk levels, decentralize actions, and keep many people involved to reduce isolation of targeted actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no one-size-fits-all; groups should evaluate personal circumstances and structure actions to mitigate risk (security practices, nonviolent direct action planning, legal preparedness). The guide emphasizes that risk is real but necessary to accept to prevent greater harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a local Indivisible group with minimal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To start a group you need two things: a handful of geographically nearby people and a shared commitment to devote a few hours a month to organizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start small, focus locally, and grow. The guide reassures that many successful groups began tiny; emphasize geography and consistent time commitments over perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify co-founders and build diverse leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Recruit a few co-founders whose social networks do not overlap too much and make leadership reflect the diversity of opposition to Trump.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose co-founders with complementary networks for maximum reach and be intentional about inclusive leadership to broaden appeal and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruit membership using multiple channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Email contacts, post on social media, message group chats, register events on Mobilize, and invite people who signaled support (e.g., yard signs) to join.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use public, discoverable recruitment (Mobilize) and personal outreach. Expect about half of RSVP’d people to attend initial meetings; leverage local hooks to attract new members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Run kickoff meetings with a bias toward action
rubrics_metrics.description: At your first meeting, agree on a name, principles, leadership roles, communication channels, and an initial strategy. Maintain momentum with a call-to-action at every meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage meeting time efficiently, set immediate next steps (date for next meeting, concrete actions), and avoid over-polishing mission statements—prioritize actionable planning and member engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide clear volunteer roles and communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign at least 1–2 coordinators, a media/social contact, and 1–2 people to track elected schedules. Choose a communication platform (email, Signal, WhatsApp, Discord, etc.) that the group will use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Role clarity prevents burnout and improves follow-through. Pick communication tools members will actually use and keep channels for leadership vs whole-group discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop consistent meeting rituals and cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a regular meeting schedule (weekly, biweekly, or monthly) so members have a dependable space for engagement and strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency builds community and resilience during upheaval. At the first meeting, set the next meeting date and tentative cadence to create expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose concrete first actions to build momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with community gatherings to process events, use the guide to plan local priorities, or create social events (bonfires, potlucks, dances) to recruit and retain members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix organizing with community-building; sample actions include a Gathering Guide event, local outreach, and creative social activities that welcome newcomers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register your group and use national Indivisible supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Register your group on Indivisible’s map and leverage national programs: distributed fundraising, GROW Grants, IndivisiGather reimbursements, and reimbursements for big actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration increases visibility and access to financial support. Use national grant programs for capacity-building and reimbursements for larger coordinated actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use national organizing support and trainings
rubrics_metrics.description: Access the Group Support Hub, local Indivisible organizers, national trainings (starting a group, recruitment, leadership), and organizer office hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tap national organizer resources for planning, troubleshooting, and coordination across groups. Contact supportteam@indivisible.org to connect to local organizers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use press and strategic communications support
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with Indivisible’s press team to get media lists, draft advisories/press releases, practice interviews, and pitch reporters for local hooks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earned media amplifies local impact on legislators; ask press@indivisible.org for support and practice media engagements to increase coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with national calls to action and coordinate with other groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in national calls, Weeks of Action, surgical campaigns, and connect with other local Indivisible groups and caucuses (Raucous Rural, National BIPOC Caucus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordination multiplies impact: learn best practices from peers, join regional projects, and use national calls for strategic guidance and larger-scale mobilization.
